claim: γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the human brain and can be measured with magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS).
source: γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the human brain and can be measured with magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about GABA's role and MRS measurement capability.

claim: Conflicting accounts report decreases and increases in cortical GABA levels across the lifespan.
source: Conflicting accounts report decreases and increases in cortical GABA levels across the lifespan.
evidence: This statement summarizes the literature review findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: No single study to date has included the entire lifespan.
source: No single study to date has included the entire lifespan.
evidence: This is based on the systematic review of literature conducted by the authors.

claim: Eight suitable datasets were integrated to generate a model of the trajectory of frontal GABA estimates across the lifespan.
source: In this study, eight suitable datasets were integrated to generate a model of the trajectory of frontal GABA estimates (as reported through edited MRS; both expressed as ratios and in institutional units) across the lifespan.
evidence: This describes the methodology and data used in the current study.

claim: Data were fit using both a log-normal curve and a nonparametric spline as regression models using a multi-level Bayesian model utilizing the Stan language.
source: Data were fit using both a log-normal curve and a nonparametric spline as regression models using a multi-level Bayesian model utilizing the Stan language.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods used in the analysis.

claim: Integrated data show that an asymmetric lifespan trajectory of frontal GABA measures involves an early period of increase, followed by a period of stability during early adulthood, with a gradual decrease during adulthood and aging.
source: Integrated data show that an asymmetric lifespan trajectory of frontal GABA measures involves an early period of increase, followed by a period of stability during early adulthood, with a gradual decrease during adulthood and aging that is described well by both spline and log-normal models.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study based on the data analysis.

claim: The asymmetric lifespan trajectory is described well by both spline and log-normal models.
source: Integrated data show that an asymmetric lifespan trajectory of frontal GABA measures involves an early period of increase, followed by a period of stability during early adulthood, with a gradual decrease during adulthood and aging that is described well by both spline and log-normal models.
evidence: This is based on the statistical modeling results presented in the study.

claim: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the human nervous system and plays a fundamental role in central nervous system function.
source: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the human nervous system and plays a fundamental role in central nervous system function (Buzsáki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Aging-related changes in GABA are consistently associated with cognitive and neurophysiological outcomes that change across the lifespan.
source: These studies have found that aging-related changes in GABA are consistently associated with cognitive and neurophysiological outcomes that change across the lifespan.
evidence: This is based on the review of multiple studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: Some studies have reported increases in GABA as age increases in left frontal cortex between 13 and 53 years.
source: Some have reported increases in GABA as age increases in left frontal cortex between 13 and 53 years (Ghisleni et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Others have reported decreases in medial frontal GABA in various age ranges.
source: Others have reported decreases in medial frontal GABA (Marenco et al., 2018, 18–55 years; Porges et al., 2017a, 43–92 years; Rowland et al., 2016, 16–62 years) and GABA/creatine plus phosphocreatine (Cr+PCr) (Gao et al., 2013, 20–76 years).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Gao and Porges show the same aging-related decrease in midline parietal GABA/Cr+PCr and GABA, respectively.
source: Gao and Porges show the same aging-related decrease in midline parietal GABA/Cr+PCr and GABA, respectively, as does (Simmonite et al., 2019) for GABA/Cr+PCr in occipital regions (18–87 years).
evidence: This is based on citations to specific studies.

claim: Still others reported no significant aging-related changes in GABA or GABA/Cr+PCr.
source: Still others reported no significant aging-related changes in GABA (Aufhaus et al., 2013, 21–53 years) or GABA/Cr+PCr (Mikkelsen et al., 2017, 18–48 years).
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: All studies were cross-sectional rather than looking at within-subject change in GABA with age.
source: Of interest, all studies were cross-sectional rather than looking at within-subject change in GABA with age.
evidence: This is based on the review of study designs in the literature.

claim: Both Porges et al., 2017a and Gao et al., 2013 focus on adults through advanced age and both report aging-related decrease in GABA.
source: For example, both Porges et al., 2017a and Gao et al., 2013 focus on adults through advanced age and both report aging-related decrease in GABA.
evidence: This is based on citations to specific studies.

claim: The apparent conflict in the relationship between GABA and age in the literature is the result of restricted age ranges within each study.
source: Here, we predict that this apparent conflict in the relationship between GABA and age in the literature is the result of restricted age ranges within each study and that the various linear relationships are part of larger, non-linear asymmetric lifespan trajectory of GABA with age.
evidence: This is the hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their analysis.

claim: Non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan have been shown in inhibition-dependent behavior.
source: This would be consistent with prior work showing non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan including inhibition-dependent behavior (Williams et al., 1999), GAD65 expression (Pinto et al., 2010), cortical thinning (Fjell et al., 2019; Walhovd et al., 2016; Raznahan et al., 2011), and white matter development (Lebel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan have been shown in GAD65 expression.
source: This would be consistent with prior work showing non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan including inhibition-dependent behavior (Williams et al., 1999), GAD65 expression (Pinto et al., 2010), cortical thinning (Fjell et al., 2019; Walhovd et al., 2016; Raznahan et al., 2011), and white matter development (Lebel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan have been shown in cortical thinning.
source: This would be consistent with prior work showing non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan including inhibition-dependent behavior (Williams et al., 1999), GAD65 expression (Pinto et al., 2010), cortical thinning (Fjell et al., 2019; Walhovd et al., 2016; Raznahan et al., 2011), and white matter development (Lebel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan have been shown in white matter development.
source: This would be consistent with prior work showing non-linear relationships with age across the human lifespan including inhibition-dependent behavior (Williams et al., 1999), GAD65 expression (Pinto et al., 2010), cortical thinning (Fjell et al., 2019; Walhovd et al., 2016; Raznahan et al., 2011), and white matter development (Lebel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: An exploratory LOESS regression for macromolecule-suppressed medial-frontal GABA × age in healthy controls reported by Rowland et al., 2016 suggests a non-linear asymmetric lifespan trajectory.
source: With respect to MRS, this prediction of a non-linear asymmetric lifespan trajectory, with an increase during childhood and aging-associated gradual decrease, is further suggested by an exploratory LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing) regression for macromolecule-suppressed medial-frontal GABA × age in healthy controls reported by Rowland et al., 2016.
evidence: This is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: The majority of MRS studies of GABA at 3 T have utilized J-difference editing to selectively 'edit' the GABA signal.
source: The majority of MRS studies of GABA at 3 T have utilized J-difference editing to selectively 'edit' the GABA signal (e.g. Mullins et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents common practice in the field.

claim: Editing is necessary at 3 T due to the low concentration of GABA in the human brain (1–2 mM).
source: Editing is necessary at 3 T due to the low concentration of GABA in the human brain (1–2 mM) (Harris et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: The most widely used J-difference editing MRS technique is MEGA-PRESS.
source: The most widely used J-difference editing MRS technique is MEGA-PRESS (Mescher et al., 1998), in which a GABA-selective editing pulse at 1.9 ppm is applied in half of the experiment (edit-ON and is coupled to a GABA signal at 3 ppm) but not in the other half (edit-OFF, where ON and OFF acquisitions are typically interleaved).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The difference spectrum shows only those signals affected by the frequency-selective editing pulse, revealing a GABA signal at 3 ppm.
source: The difference spectrum (ON-OFF acquisitions) shows only those signals affected by the frequency-selective editing pulse, revealing a GABA signal at 3 ppm.
evidence: This describes the technical principle of the MEGA-PRESS method.

claim: The difference spectrum is complicated by a macromolecule signal at 3 ppm which is co-edited, resulting in a 'GABA+' signal.
source: The difference spectrum is further complicated by a macromolecule signal at 3 ppm which is coupled to another macromolecule signal at 1.7 ppm and thus falls within the envelope of the editing pulse, resulting in a co-edited macromolecule signal as part of the 3 ppm GABA signal (Edden et al., 2014; Henry et al., 2001). Consequently, most studies refer to the GABA signal as 'GABA+'.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Measurement of the GABA-edited signal in humans requires a large voxel (most commonly 27 cm3) to keep acquisition times reasonable and to provide an adequate signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Due to its low concentration, measurement of the GABA-edited signal in humans requires a large voxel (most commonly 27 cm3; Mullins et al., 2014; Peek et al., 2020) to keep acquisition times reasonable (~10 min) and to provide an adequate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (Mikkelsen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Studies have suggested that the majority of the GABA measured using MRS reflects intracellular somatic levels rather than synaptic or extracellular levels.
source: However, studies have suggested that the majority of the GABA measured using MRS reflects intracellular somatic levels rather than synaptic or extracellular levels since MRS measures of GABA were associated with expression of the 67 isoform of glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) which is predominantly present in the soma of the neuron (Marenco et al., 2011; Rae, 2014; Stagg et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The GABA signal is considered to be reflective of inhibitory tone.
source: As such, the GABA signal is considered to be reflective of inhibitory tone (Rae, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: GABA levels measured via MRS in young adults at rest have been reported to be stable for up to 7 months.
source: GABA levels measured via MRS in young adults at rest have been reported to be stable for up to 7 months (Near et al., 2014) and do not exhibit a diurnal rhythm (Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: GABA levels measured via MRS do not exhibit a diurnal rhythm.
source: GABA levels measured via MRS in young adults at rest have been reported to be stable for up to 7 months (Near et al., 2014) and do not exhibit a diurnal rhythm (Evans et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD.
source: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD (Bollmann et al., 2015; Edden et al., 2012), autism spectrum disorder (Cochran et al., 2015; Drenthen et al., 2016; Gaetz et al., 2014; Puts et al., 2017), and Tourette syndrome (Puts et al., 2015), as well as in other neurological and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in autism spectrum disorder.
source: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD (Bollmann et al., 2015; Edden et al., 2012), autism spectrum disorder (Cochran et al., 2015; Drenthen et al., 2016; Gaetz et al., 2014; Puts et al., 2017), and Tourette syndrome (Puts et al., 2015), as well as in other neurological and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in Tourette syndrome.
source: Alterations of GABA levels are seen in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD (Bollmann et al., 2015; Edden et al., 2012), autism spectrum disorder (Cochran et al., 2015; Drenthen et al., 2016; Gaetz et al., 2014; Puts et al., 2017), and Tourette syndrome (Puts et al., 2015), as well as in other neurological and psychiatric disorders.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Port et al., 2017 and Silveri et al., 2013 report a maturational increase in GABA+/Cr+PCr in typically developing children and adolescents.
source: Port et al., 2017 and Silveri et al., 2013 report a maturational increase in GABA+/Cr+PCr in typically developing children and adolescents.
evidence: This is based on citations to specific studies.

claim: Human autopsy data describes large changes in both GABA synthesis and receptor expression.
source: Human autopsy data describes large changes in both GABA synthesis and receptor expression (Pinto et al., 2010) and animal models describe a shift in GABA from excitatory to inhibitory (Leonzino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Animal models describe a shift in GABA from excitatory to inhibitory.
source: Human autopsy data describes large changes in both GABA synthesis and receptor expression (Pinto et al., 2010) and animal models describe a shift in GABA from excitatory to inhibitory (Leonzino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Imaging of MRS of GABA is highly sensitive to motion.
source: For example, it is well established that imaging of MRS of GABA is highly sensitive to motion (Edden et al., 2016; Mullins et al., 2014), thus compounding the challenges involved when imaging pediatric cohorts.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Mikkelsen et al., 2017 conducted a multisite study collecting GABA+ levels in 272 participants between 18 and 35 years of age.
source: Mikkelsen et al., 2017 conducted a multisite study collecting GABA+ levels in 272 participants between 18 and 35 years of age, providing a substantial dataset to assess this relationship.
evidence: This is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: There was no aging-related increase or decrease between age and GABA+/Cr+PCr in adults between 18 and 35 years of age in the Mikkelsen study.
source: There was no aging-related increase or decrease between age and GABA+/Cr+PCr [χ2(7)=3.52, pboot = 0.31] in this large cohort of adults between 18 and 35 years of age.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data from the Mikkelsen study.

claim: Most MRS of GABA studies that investigate aging populations report a decrease in cortical GABA as a function of age in both frontal and parietal voxels.
source: Most, if not all, MRS of GABA studies that investigate aging populations report a decrease in cortical GABA as a function of age in both frontal (Gao et al., 2013; Porges et al., 2017a) and parietal (Gao et al., 2013) voxels.
evidence: This is based on citations to multiple studies.

claim: A linear trend over the entire lifespan is not appropriate for describing GABA changes with age.
source: Although a linear trend may provide an approximate summary over short periods of time, a linear trend over the entire lifespan is not appropriate.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of the data presented in the study.

claim: In six of the eight datasets, the linear trend explained less than 20% of the variance.
source: In six of the eight datasets, the linear trend explained less than 20% of the variance.
evidence: This is based on the statistical analysis presented in Table 1.

claim: The overall time course is characterized by an increase in GABA during childhood, followed by a plateau from adolescence through midlife, and then a gradual decline from approximately 40 years onward.
source: Overall, this time course is characterized by an increase in GABA during childhood, followed by a plateau from adolescence through midlife, and then a gradual decline from approximately 40 years onward.
evidence: This is based on the spline model results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The estimated scaling factors line up with the score ranges consistent with those reported in the Big GABA series of meta-analyses.
source: For example, our three Cr+PCr-referenced datasets (Gao, Mikkelsen, and Simmonite) all yielded scaling factors well below 1.0, consistent with the measurement scale typically observed in GABA+/Cr+PCr studies (Mikkelsen et al., 2017), whereas water-referenced data yielded scaling factors one or two orders of magnitude larger than Cr+PCr-referenced data, also consistent with typical measurement (Mikkelsen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current study's results with published findings.

claim: When datasets are left out in LOO cross-validation, the general shape of both models remains the same.
source: Figure 4 shows that when datasets are left out, the general shape of both models remains the same, with wider 95% credible intervals for the oldest of age due to limited available data.
evidence: This is based on the LOO analysis results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overall pattern of a negative slope in late age is unlikely to be driven by Cr+PCr differences.
source: This suggests that the overall pattern of a negative slope in late age is unlikely to be driven by Cr+PCr differences, as the data contributed by Porges et al., 2017a made the largest contribution to this slope (having the most observations to contribute) and relied on a water-based reference method.
evidence: This is based on inference from the LOO analysis and consideration of reference methods.

claim: A decline in GABAergic interneurons with age has been widely reported in animal models.
source: Indeed, a decline in GABAergic interneurons with age has been widely reported in animal models (Hua et al., 2008; Stanley et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Post-mortem data from human samples showed a reduction in GAD65 in visual cortex, suggesting reduced GABA production with aging.
source: Post-mortem data from human samples showed a reduction in the 65 isoform of GAD (the enzyme responsible for the production of GABA, GAD) in visual cortex, suggesting reduced GABA production with aging (Pinto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Non-linear trajectories have been reported in aging effects of total gray matter.
source: Non-linear trajectories have been reported in aging effects of total gray matter (Lenroot et al., 2007; Sussman et al., 2016) and cortical thickness (Shaw et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Diffusion tensor imaging studies show non-linear aging-related differences through childhood and adolescence.
source: Diffusion tensor imaging studies show non-linear aging-related differences through childhood and adolescence (Lebel and Beaulieu, 2011), with an 'inverted U-shaped' trajectory that peaks at approximately 40 years of age (Bendlin et al., 2010; Good et al., 2001; Lebel et al., 2012; Westlye et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A similar trajectory pattern for cognitive abilities is reported in memory, verbal ability, and inductive reasoning.
source: A similar trajectory pattern for cognitive abilities is reported in memory, verbal ability, and inductive reasoning (Kobayashi et al., 2015), as well as word recall, verbal fluency, math skills (Whitley et al., 2016), and behavioral inhibition (Williams et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: GABA is thought to be linked to the myelination of frontal white matter trajectories by controlling oligodendrocyte precursor cell activity through the developmental phase.
source: GABA is thought to be linked to the myelination of frontal white matter trajectories by controlling oligodendrocyte precursor cell activity through the developmental phase (Ghisleni et al., 2015; Vélez-Fort et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Astrocytes have been shown to mediate plasticity of rodent hippocampus and visual cortex.
source: This potentiation-like mechanism of cortical GABA is supported by studies where astrocytes have been shown to mediate plasticity of rodent hippocampus (Kang et al., 1998) and visual cortex (Chen et al., 2012), suggesting a possible potentiation-like mechanism of cortical GABA concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: GABA levels as measured with MRS have been shown to relate to expression of the GAD1 gene.
source: In addition, upregulation of GAD could lead to increased production of GABA and indeed, GABA levels as measured with MRS have been shown to relate to expression of the GAD1 gene (Marenco et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: GABAergic neuronal function is reported to become more efficient through synaptic pruning and long-term depression during development.
source: GABAergic neuronal function is reported to become more efficient through synaptic pruning and long-term depression during development (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Wagner and Alger, 1995; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Rodent studies have shown a reduction in the number of interneurons expressing GAD in the medial prefrontal cortex, accompanied by altered spatial working memory.
source: Rodent studies have shown a reduction in the number of interneurons expressing GAD in the medial prefrontal cortex. These reductions were accompanied by altered spatial working memory, linking altered GABA function to altered behavior in aging (Spiegel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Rodent models of cognitive decline have shown altered function at both GABA-A and GABA-B receptors.
source: Additionally, rodent models of cognitive decline have shown altered function at both GABA-A and GABA-B receptors (McQuail et al., 2015), as well as a reduction in GABAergic neurons in cats and monkeys (Hua et al., 2008; Leventhal et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Using GAD labeling methodology in the human visual cortex, GAD65 has been reported to increase early in life and gradually decrease during aging.
source: Using GAD labeling methodology in the human visual cortex, GAD65 has been reported to increase early in life and gradually decrease during aging (Pinto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: GAD67 has been shown to be stable across the lifespan.
source: Provocatively, they show GAD67 to be stable across the lifespan.
evidence: This is based on the findings from Pinto et al., 2010.

claim: A recent cross-sectional exploration found reduction in GAD65, but not GAD67 in the superior temporal gyrus of females (but not males).
source: Similarly, a recent cross-sectional exploration of sex differences in young and old adults found reduction in GAD65, but not GAD67 in the superior temporal gyrus of females (but not males). No change in GAD65 or GAD67 was found in other regions, though prefrontal cortex was not reported (Pandya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Medial temporal lobe reductions in GAD65, but not GAD67, have been reported in Alzheimer's disease.
source: We are unaware of other reports of normal human aging-related differences in GAD; however medial temporal lobe reductions (prefrontal cortex was not reported) in GAD65, but not GAD67, have also been reported in Alzheimer's disease (Schwab et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Regional differences in GABA are not homogeneous.
source: It can be assumed that regional differences in GABA are not homogeneous.
evidence: This is a reasonable inference based on known brain heterogeneity.

claim: The Cr+PCr signal at 3.05 ppm has minimal chemical shift from the GABA signal at 3 ppm.
source: For instance, the Cr+PCr at 3.05 ppm has minimal chemical shift from the GABA signal at 3 ppm (Mullins et al., 2014) and is acquired during the MEGA-PRESS sequence.
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents technical knowledge.

claim: A small number of studies have looked at the relationship between Cr+PCr and age showing an increase or no change with age.
source: A small number of studies have looked at the relationship between Cr+PCr and age (Ding et al., 2016; Lind et al., 2020) showing an increase or no change with age (for a review, see Cleeland et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Gao et al. investigated both GABA/Cr+PCr and GABA/NAA and found similar aging-related reductions in GABA referenced to both molecules.
source: However, Gao et al. investigated both GABA/Cr+PCr and GABA/NAA and found similar aging-related reductions in GABA referenced to both molecules.
evidence: This is based on citation to a specific study.

claim: NAA has been shown to consistently decrease in aging.
source: Given that NAA has, in contrast to the increase of Cr+PCr, been shown to consistently decrease in aging (Cleeland et al., 2019), it makes it unlikely that Gao's aging-related reduction was solely driven by a Cr+PCr increase during aging.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Voxel tissue composition has a significant impact on the quantification of GABA levels.
source: It is well known that voxel tissue composition has a significant impact on the quantification of GABA levels (Harris et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: None of the studies included in this review showed significant differences in segmented tissue content with age.
source: Interestingly, none of the studies included in this review showed significant differences in segmented tissue content with age.
evidence: This is based on review of the included studies.

claim: Other studies showed that aging-related differences in GABA depend on tissue correction due to atrophy being common in older participants.
source: This is surprising because other studies (Maes et al., 2018; Porges et al., 2017b) showed that aging-related differences in GABA depend on tissue correction due to atrophy being common in older participants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In water-referenced studies of aging-related differences in older cohorts, accounting for CSF in the tissue correction approach does not remove a significant relationship between age and cortical GABA.
source: In water-referenced studies of aging-related differences in older cohorts (where bulk tissue changes are most likely to impact this relationship), accounting for CSF in the tissue correction approach does not remove a significant relationship between age and cortical GABA (Porges et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Studies used a variety of scanner vendors, which is known to contribute to between-site variability.
source: As for other methodological differences (Table 2 and Table 3), studies used a variety of scanner vendors: a variation that is known to contribute to between-site variability (Mikkelsen et al., 2017) but is unlikely to lead to substantial difference in the age relationship.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: A systematic literature search was performed to retrieve studies in which MRS of GABA using the MEGA-PRESS method was collected in the human brain from voxels that included the frontal lobe.
source: A systematic literature search was performed in two iterations by BF and EP to retrieve studies in which MRS of GABA using the MEGA-PRESS method was collected in the human brain from voxels that included the frontal lobe.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the systematic review.

claim: The search was conducted on April 2, 2019, resulting in a total of 271 studies, of which 55 were relevant.
source: The search was conducted on April 2, 2019, resulting in a total of 271 studies. Out of these, 55 were relevant.
evidence: This describes the results of the systematic search.

claim: Of the 55 relevant studies retrieved in the systematic search, only seven included figures suitable for data extraction or had data freely available in available online repositories.
source: Of the 55 relevant studies retrieved in the systematic search, only seven included figures suitable for data extraction or had data freely available in available online repositories.
evidence: This describes the results of the eligibility assessment.

claim: One dataset was only partly published but was supplied in full by authors of this manuscript, for a total of eight datasets.
source: One dataset was only partly published (Puts et al., 2017) but was supplied in full by authors of this manuscript NP and RAEE, for a total of eight datasets.
evidence: This describes the data sources for the meta-analysis.

claim: All eight studies included in the systematic review included both male and female participants.
source: All eight studies included in the systematic review included both male and female participants, although the pediatric data were somewhat skewed to include more males.
evidence: This is based on review of the included studies.

claim: No data were excluded based on acquisition parameters as assessed with the MRS-Q.
source: No data were excluded based on acquisition parameters as assessed with the MRS-Q.
evidence: This describes the quality assessment process.

claim: With the exception of two publications, the age-by-GABA relationship was not a primary outcome and was therefore unlikely to have been a driver of publication bias in the majority of studies included.
source: With the exception of two publications (Gao et al., 2013; Porges et al., 2017a), the age-by-GABA relationship was not a primary outcome and was therefore unlikely to have been a driver of publication bias in the majority of studies included.
evidence: This is based on review of the included studies and assessment of publication bias risk.

claim: Individual data points were extracted from figures using WebPlotDigitizer.
source: Individual data points were extracted from figures using WebPlotDigitizer (Rohatgi, 2019).
evidence: This describes the data extraction methodology.

claim: None of the data included were corrected for voxel tissue fractions.
source: None of the data included were corrected for voxel tissue fractions (see Discussion).
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the included data.
